title: Vatican I, 1870
hook: the pope is protected from error only when solemnly defining faith or morals for the whole Church, rarely used

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tridentine: of Trent, the seminaries, the catechism and the Mass book. Your line was four hundred years. Today we skip ahead to the next council, held at the Vatican itself. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

A pope says he likes a film. A pope gives an interview on a plane. A pope picks a soccer team. Somewhere, within the hour, a headline asks whether Catholics now have to agree with him. The question comes from a word the First Vatican Council defined, and it is often misheard. It does not mean the pope is never wrong. It means something much smaller and much stranger. Today's word: infallibility.
screen: `A POPE ON A PLANE.` → `DO CATHOLICS HAVE TO AGREE?` → `INFALLIBILITY.`

segments.voice: Start with what it isn't. Infallibility is not sinlessness. Popes go to confession too. It isn't about a pope's opinions, his homilies, his interviews, or his politics either. Now, what the council actually said. Its constitution on the papacy, called Pastor Aeternus, teaches that when the Roman Pontiff speaks ex cathedra, from the chair, meaning when, as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, he defines a teaching on faith or morals to be held by the whole Church, he is kept from error by the help God promised to Peter. Every one of those conditions has to be there. Next, the reason given. The council pointed to Jesus's words at the Last Supper, in the Douay-Rheims: "But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and thou, being once converted, confirm thy brethren." And the same document says the Holy Spirit was not promised so the popes could make known new teaching, but so they could guard and faithfully explain what was handed down. Infallibility is a guardrail, not an engine. Finally, how often. Catholic teachers point out that solemn definitions like this are rare; the example people usually give is Pope Pius the Twelfth defining Mary's Assumption. Other Christians, Orthodox and Protestant, do not accept this teaching, and some Catholics at the council itself argued that defining it was unwise. That's today's line: rarer than people think.
screen: `NOT SINLESSNESS, NOT OPINIONS.` · `EX CATHEDRA: FAITH OR MORALS, FOR ALL.` · `CONFIRM THY BRETHREN.` · `A GUARDRAIL, NOT AN ENGINE.` · then, large: `RARER THAN PEOPLE THINK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn the narrow meaning. For the sit, walk slowly through the conditions, one per breath. The pope. Speaking as teacher of all Christians. Defining. Faith or morals. For the whole Church. Then let go of everything that falls outside them: the interviews, the opinions, the plane rides. If you pray, you can pray for the pope, in Jesus's words, that his faith fail not. The bell holds the time.
Infallibility. Protection from error when the pope solemnly defines faith or morals for the whole Church; not sinlessness, and not his every word. Today's word.
Your line: rarer than people think. Today, when you see a headline about something a pope said, ask the five questions before you decide what it means. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics distinguish a pope's solemn definitions, which the Church holds as infallible, from his ordinary teaching, homilies and personal opinions, and Catholic catechisms explain the narrow conditions set by the First Vatican Council.

fork.setup: a pope shares his view on a film in an interview. a friend asks if Catholics must now agree. what's the answer by Vatican I's terms?

no, it's not a solemn definition of faith or morals.

fork.reveal: Vatican I limits infallibility to solemn definitions on faith or morals for the whole Church, so an opinion on a film falls outside it.

notes: The carry 'rarer than people think' is fixed by the index. The voice says only that solemn definitions are 'rare' per Catholic teachers and gives the Assumption as the usual example; no count is stated. Confirm this is acceptable.
Hook says the word 'gets misheard all the time'; an editor may soften further.
Pastor Aeternus ch. 4 is paraphrased (ex cathedra conditions; Spirit not promised for new doctrine). Confirm summary.
'Some Catholics at the council itself argued that defining it was unwise' refers to the inopportunist minority; confirm phrasing.
Original: Latin 'infallibilitas' and pronunciation (ecclesiastical Latin) — confirm. The constitution's text uses the ablative 'infallibilitate'.
The year 1870 appears only in the index title, not in the voice.
Editor: softened 'misheard all the time' to 'often misheard'; cut the uncited 'the Church has never taught' claim.

Audit (2026-10-01): Luke 22:32 (Douay-Rheims) checked and is the verse Pastor Aeternus ch. 4 cites; ex cathedra conditions and 'not to make known new doctrine' fairly paraphrased; carry's 'five questions' matches the five conditions in the practice; no change.
